questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a review protocol commits to in advance
questions.learningObjective: state what a protocol fixes before the search begins
questions.stem: A review team writes a protocol before searching any database. Which combination belongs in it, and why?

options.text: The eligibility criteria, the search sources, the screening procedure and the risk-of-bias tool, because deciding them in advance stops the team fitting the review to the studies it happens to find
The expected direction of the pooled effect and the studies that will be included, because the protocol should let the team commit to a result in advance
options.misconception: treats a protocol as a licence to pre-announce the answer

options.text: The main analysis code and the output figures, because a protocol must show reviewers exactly what the final tables will look like
options.misconception: asks a protocol to contain the finished results rather than the plan

options.text: The screeners to be hired and their pay rate, because staffing is the largest source of variation in how a screening is carried out
options.misconception: puts a resource decision in the list and omits every methodological commitment

questions.explanation: A protocol is a dated public record of the decisions a review will make, written before the evidence is seen, and the whole value of it is that the decisions cannot be adjusted once the results are known. Registering the eligibility criteria, the databases to be searched, how records will be screened, which risk-of-bias tool will be applied and how disagreements get resolved means a reader can tell whether a study was set aside for a reason decided in advance or for a reason invented afterwards, and that single question is what separates a systematic review from a well-organised literature survey. Option B describes pre-commitment to a result, which is the opposite purpose. Option C asks for artefacts that exist only after the work is done. Option D omits every methodological decision.
questions.hint: Ask which decisions a reader would suspect were made after the results were known.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Boolean structure of a search string
questions.learningObjective: read the grouping and truncation of a search string
questions.stem: A reviewer enters the string (adolescen* OR teen*) AND (smok* OR tobacco) AND "policy implement*", and 1,180 records come back. What does the string's structure tell you about what has been asked of the database?

options.text: Every record matches at least one term from each of the three bracketed groups, so the search asks for policy on adolescent tobacco use rather than for either topic alone
Every record matches all of the six terms at once, since the keyword operator requires each word to appear in the record
options.misconception: reads the operator as demanding every term within a group rather than any

options.text: The search asks for records about adolescents or about tobacco, since the keyword operator only binds the two groups it joins
options.misconception: collapses a three-part conjunction into a two-part disjunction

options.text: The search is restricted to records written in English, because the quoted phrase indicates the database's language setting
options.misconception: reads a phrase-search construct as a language filter

questions.explanation: A search string is a logic expression about sets of records, and the three bracketed groups joined by the keyword operator require membership in all of them, so a record survives only if it carries at least one adolescent synonym, at least one tobacco synonym and the policy phrase, which is what makes the 1,180 records a set about policy rather than about either topic alone. The trailing wildcards and the phrase quotes do the remaining work: they widen the vocabulary so that a term's plural and inflected forms are caught, and they force the two policy words to sit together rather than merely appearing somewhere in a long record. The number 1,180 is uninterpretable without knowing the structure that produced it, which is why a good review records the string, the fields, the date and the counts at each stage. Option B confuses within-group and between-group logic, option C collapses a conjunction into a disjunction, and option D invents a function for phrase quotes.
questions.hint: Trace one record through the expression: it must survive every group joined by the keyword operator.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Operationalising an inclusion criterion
questions.learningObjective: turn a vague eligibility statement into a rule that can be applied twice the same way
questions.stem: A review protocol states an inclusion criterion of studies with adequate policy context. The first screeners disagree about a third of the records. What is the defect in the criterion?

options.text: Adequate is unobservable, so two screeners can apply it differently, and the remedy is a stated threshold such as a named country list or a minimum period of policy in force
The criterion is ambiguous but harmless, because a third of disagreements is an ordinary rate of screening disagreement in any review
options.misconception: dismisses a defect on the grounds that disagreement is routine

options.text: The criterion is too strict, because no policy studies specify their context clearly enough to satisfy a stated threshold
options.misconception: mistakes a vague criterion for an unduly demanding one

options.text: The criterion is fine, but the team needs more screeners, since additional readers will resolve the ambiguity without changing it
options.misconception: suggests adding labour in place of making the rule observable

questions.explanation: An inclusion criterion is only usable if two people independently applying it reach the same verdict, and adequate fails that test because it names no observable feature of the record, so a screener is left to decide from impression and impressions differ. The remedy is not a better reader or a longer shift but a criterion expressed in terms a reader can point at, whether that is a named list of jurisdictions, a minimum number of months a policy had been in force before data collection, or a stated threshold of what counts as the population of interest, and the criterion should then be pilot-screened on a sample of records to check that it now produces agreement. Option B mistakes a defect for noise. Option C attacks a threshold that does not yet exist. Option D adds labour while leaving the cause untouched.
questions.hint: A criterion is only usable if two people can point at the same feature of a record and reach the same verdict.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Recording the reason a full text was excluded
questions.learningObjective: explain what a recorded exclusion reason allows a reader to check
questions.stem: A review reports 155 full texts were retrieved and 43 were included, with 112 excluded. In what circumstance does reporting that count strengthen the review rather than merely fill a table?

options.text: When each of the 112 exclusions carries a reason from the protocol's own criteria, so a reader can see which criterion removed them and whether any single criterion removed almost everything
Whenever the 112 exclusions are named in the text, since naming excluded work is itself a mark of thoroughness
options.misconception: mistakes the presence of a count for the presence of a reason

options.text: Only when the 112 exclusions are published in full, since a reader who cannot read the excluded studies cannot judge the decision
options.misconception: assumes a reader needs the excluded full texts rather than the reasons for excluding them

options.text: When the number 112 is smaller than the number excluded at title screening, since a large fall at full text signals a careful reading
options.misconception: treats a stage count as evidence of rigour regardless of any recorded reason

questions.explanation: A count tells a reader that 112 studies were set aside and nothing about whether they deserved it, so the count becomes informative only when it is broken down by the criteria that set them aside, and a breakdown serves two purposes at once: it lets a reader check that no criterion quietly removed most of the field, and it exposes the reviews failure to find anything when one criterion excluded every record, which is a signal that the criterion was written for a literature that does not exist. The reasons also have to be mutually exclusive and drawn from the protocol, or the same record can be counted twice and the arithmetic stops meaning anything. Option B mistakes a number for a justification. Option C asks for the excluded papers rather than for the reasoning. Option D reads rigour out of a stage transition with no reasons attached.
questions.hint: A count only becomes evidence once it is broken down by the criterion that produced it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a screening stage needs two independent screeners
questions.learningObjective: state what inter-rater agreement establishes at screening
questions.stem: A review screens every record twice, independently, and reconciles disagreements by discussion with a third reader. What does this arrangement establish, and what does it not?

options.text: It establishes that the criteria can be applied consistently enough for the included set to be reproducible, though it does not by itself make the criteria correct or unbiased
It establishes that the included set is unbiased, because two independent readers cannot share the same blind spot
options.misconception: claims agreement removes systematic bias from a criterion

options.text: It establishes that the criteria are the right ones, because a criterion two readers can agree on must be a criterion that was written well
options.misconception: treats reliability as a test of whether a criterion is the correct one

options.text: It establishes that the search retrieved everything relevant, because consistent screening cannot lose a record both readers missed
options.misconception: extends screening reliability to the completeness of the retrieval stage

questions.explanation: Screening is where a review's inclusion decisions are made, and two independent readers turn those decisions into something a second team could reproduce, which is what the agreement statistic measures: the extent to which the criteria yield the same verdict twice rather than how many records there are. What agreement cannot reach is whether the criteria are the right ones, because two readers can apply a biased criterion identically, and both can agree to exclude every study on a topic the review should have covered. That is why a report gives the agreement statistic alongside the criteria themselves and the reason codes, so a reader can inspect the rule as well as the consistency of its application. Option B mistakes consistency for fairness. Option C mistakes it for correctness. Option D confuses applying a rule well with having retrieved the right records to apply it to.
questions.hint: Reliability is a property of the application of a rule, not of the rule's content.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Cohen kappa for two screeners
questions.learningObjective: compute chance-corrected agreement between two screeners
questions.stem: Two screeners independently judge 100 records. Both include 40 records, both exclude 42, the first alone includes 10 and the second alone excludes 8. Give Cohen's kappa for this pair, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Observed agreement is the 82 records the two screeners judged identically, which is 0.82, and because that is higher than the 0.50 expected from two screeners each including about half the records by chance, the excess is divided by the 0.50 still available, giving (0.82 - 0.50) divided by (1 - 0.50), which is 0.64. The correction is what makes the number mean anything, since with margins this even a coin-tossing pair would agree half the time and reporting 0.82 raw would read as excellent screening when it is only chance. The value is substantial agreement rather than near-perfect, and a review with a kappa near 0.64 should look again at whether its criteria are specific enough to be applied the same way twice.
questions.hint: Subtract the agreement two random screeners would produce from the agreement observed, then divide by what was left to win.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Inverse-variance weighting in a fixed-effect meta-analysis
questions.learningObjective: compute a pooled estimate under inverse-variance weighting
questions.stem: Three studies report log effects of 0.30, 0.10 and 0.50 with standard errors of 0.20, 0.10 and 0.30. A fixed-effect meta-analysis weights each by the inverse of its variance. Give the pooled estimate to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The variances are 0.04, 0.01 and 0.09, so the weights are 25, 100 and 11.11, and the weighted mean of the three effects is 23.0556 divided by 136.111, which gives 0.1694 and rounds to 0.17. The weight structure is the whole content of the calculation, because a study estimated four times as precisely as the first one is given twenty-five times the influence of the third, and the 0.10 effect is the one that moves the pooled figure most despite being the smallest of the three. Dividing the total weight into 136.111 gives a standard error of 0.0857, and an interval of 0.0014 to 0.3374, so this particular pooled estimate clears zero by a very small margin, which is worth stating rather than rounding away.
questions.hint: Weight each effect by one over its squared standard error, then take the weighted mean.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Domains covered by a risk-of-bias tool
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a risk-of-bias tool judges
questions.stem: A review applies a risk-of-bias tool with domains covering randomisation, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement and selective reporting. What is the tool estimating, and what is it not?

options.text: The risk that a study's result is distorted by the way it was designed or run, domain by domain, and not the size of its effect or the importance of its topic
The overall quality of the study, so a tool rating a trial as high risk should remove it from the review and from any pooled estimate
options.misconception: turns a per-domain judgement into a whole-study verdict and an automatic exclusion

options.text: The likelihood that a study has been published, since a study at high risk is usually the one a journal declines to print
options.misconception: redefines the tool as a test for publication, which is a separate problem in a review

options.text: The number of participants a study needed, so a tool rating a study as low risk has shown it was adequately powered for the effect it found
options.misconception: redefines the tool as a power calculation rather than a bias assessment

questions.explanation: A risk-of-bias tool walks through the features of a study's design and conduct that could bend its answer away from the truth, and the domains exist because each is a separate way that can happen: randomisation breaks down when allocation is not concealed, outcome measurement is threatened when an assessor knows the assignment, and selective reporting is suspected when the outcomes analysed differ from the outcomes registered. Evaluating the domains separately is what makes the tool useful, since a well-randomised trial that never registered its outcomes can still be at high risk, and pooling the domains into a single score throws away the only information the domains carry. Option B invites the commoner error of dropping high-risk studies wholesale rather than carrying them with a noted risk. Options C and D invent functions the tool does not have.
questions.hint: Ask what a domain describes: something that happens inside the study, not its subject matter or its sample size.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Reading asymmetry in a funnel plot
questions.learningObjective: infer what an uneven funnel shape implies about the study set
questions.stem: A funnel plot places effect size against precision, with a vertical line at the pooled estimate. Small studies cluster low on the precision axis, and on one side of the line there are far fewer of them than on the other. What is the leading explanation, and what must be ruled out first?

options.text: Small studies showing large effects are missing while small studies showing small effects are present, and small-study effects from genuine methodological differences must be ruled out first
Small studies were run in poorer settings, so the asymmetry reflects what a poor setting does to an effect rather than what was published
options.misconception: jumps to a cause other than publication before testing the simplest one

options.text: The pooled estimate is biased, so the vertical line should be drawn through the small studies rather than through all of them together
options.misconception: repositions the reference line to fit the shape and calls the difference a bias

options.text: The largest study was duplicated in the search, so the asymmetry comes from counting one study several times
options.misconception: suggests a retrieval artefact without any evidence that a duplicate exists

questions.explanation: A funnel plot draws every study at its precision and its effect, and if small studies were included whatever they found, they should scatter evenly on both sides of the pooled line, so a lopsided hole on the high-effect side is the picture that selective publication produces. The competing explanation has to be tested first because it is the more instructive one: small studies differ systematically from large ones in supervision, measurement precision and analysis flexibility, and those differences alone can pull their estimates away from the truth in a consistent direction without anyone suppressing anything. That is why a report names the asymmetry, offers the alternative account, and reports the pooled estimate again with and without the smallest studies, since a conclusion that survives both is far stronger than one that depends on a single plot shape. Options B, C and D each settle the question with an assumption the data do not support.
questions.hint: An empty side of the funnel is consistent with suppression, and one competing account must be excluded before the plot is read as suppression.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Small-study effects and publication bias are not the same
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a real small-study effect from selective publication
questions.stem: Small studies in a meta-analysis show systematically larger effects than large ones. Two explanations remain live: genuine methodological differences, and publication of small studies only when they succeed. Which comparison separates them?

options.text: Ask whether the whole registry of started studies, including the unpublished ones, shows the same size gradient, since suppression predicts a gradient in what got published and a real effect predicts one in what was run
Compare the effect sizes in the small studies with those in the large ones, since a real methodological difference must show up as a numerical gap
options.misconception: repeats the observation that prompted the question instead of testing it

options.text: Check whether the small studies used a control group, since an uncontrolled design is the usual reason small studies report larger effects
options.misconception: offers one specific cause and treats it as a decision procedure rather than a test

options.text: Recalculate the pooled estimate with the small studies removed, since a stable pooled estimate shows the effect was an artefact of the small studies
options.misconception: proposes discarding the evidence in question rather than adjudicating between causes

questions.explanation: The two explanations make opposite predictions about a set of studies that were run but never published, and a registry of completed or abandoned trials, or a comparison against a full grant record, is the one place where both can be observed: if the gradient is present in the unpublished small studies as well, then small studies genuinely produce larger estimates and nothing has been suppressed, whereas if the unpublished small studies cluster at the null, the gradient in the published set is the signature of suppression. That is why reviews register or consult a trials register rather than reasoning about the shape of a plot, since a plot cannot show the studies that are not in it. Option B restates the finding. Option C names a plausible mechanism and treats it as the answer. Option D removes the evidence the question is about.
questions.hint: Both explanations predict different things about studies that were run but never published, and that is the set to look at.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Duplicate extraction and how it is reconciled
questions.learningObjective: state how two extractions of one study are combined
questions.stem: Two reviewers independently extract the sample size, the effect measure and the risk-of-bias rating from every included study, then compare their sheets. Which arrangement actually protects the extraction?

options.text: A named rule agreed in advance for resolving each difference, and a third reviewer adjudicating the fields still in dispute, so the reconciliation is decided rather than averaged
Keeping the figure from whichever reviewer recorded it first, since the earliest reading is the one taken with the freshest attention
options.misconception: resolves disagreement by sequence rather than by argument

options.text: Averaging the two sets of numbers so that neither reviewer's work is discarded and the result stands for both
options.misconception: averages quantities that may be counts of participants or coded ratings

options.text: Discarding both sheets for any study where the reviewers differ and leaving that study out of the pooled estimate
options.misconception: drops a study for a transcription disagreement rather than correcting the field

questions.explanation: Duplicate extraction is worth doing precisely because extraction is a set of judgements about a compressed description, and two readers looking at the same paragraph can honestly differ about which arm a percentage refers to or which point on a scale a reported category maps to. A pre-agreed rule per field turns those differences into a short list, and a third reviewer settles what remains, which is what keeps the review honest: a difference is resolved by looking again at the source rather than by a rule about who was first or by splitting the difference. Averaging is the option that looks like a compromise and is not one, since a count of 240 and a count of 120 average to a number that no study reported, and a risk-of-bias rating averaged between two categories describes no domain at all. Dropping the study punishes the study for a transcription slip.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would need in order to know how the two sheets became one number.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The assumption a fixed-effect model makes
questions.learningObjective: state the assumption behind a fixed-effect estimate
questions.stem: A meta-analysis pools eight studies of the same programme in one school district under a fixed-effect model. What is the model asserting about the eight studies?

options.text: There is one true effect that all eight studies estimate, and the spread between them is sampling error, so pooling simply sharpens one estimate of it
There are eight different true effects, one per study, and the spread between them is a feature of the programmes rather than of error
options.misconception: states the random-effects position as if it were the fixed-effect one

options.text: The eight studies are equally precise, so each should carry the same weight in the pooled figure regardless of its sample size
options.misconception: assumes equal weights, which is a third thing and not what the model does

options.text: The pooled estimate applies to every setting where the programme could be used, because pooling establishes external validity on its own
options.misconception: conflates precision about an average with generalisability beyond the studied settings

questions.explanation: A fixed-effect model takes the observed spread between studies as entirely attributable to sampling error, which implies the studies share one underlying effect, and the pooled estimate is then a more precise version of that single quantity. The model is not intrinsically wrong, since it is exactly right when the studies really do share an effect and are homogeneous, and the test of that is whether the observed spread is about what chance alone would produce. The moment the observed spread exceeds what the standard errors predict, the assumption is doing damage, because the fixed-effect interval then understates the uncertainty and presents a spurious precision that later replications fail to reach. Option B is the random-effects premise. Option C is a misreading of the weighting. Option D mistakes a narrow interval for external validity.
questions.hint: Ask what the model says the spread between the study estimates is made of.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a random-effects model adds
questions.learningObjective: state what the random-effects model contributes beyond the fixed one
questions.stem: A fixed-effect and a random-effects analysis of the same eight studies give pooled estimates of 0.30 and 0.18, and the random-effects interval is markedly wider. What has the second model done?

options.text: Charged each study for the spread between them as well as for its own error, so the interval widens and the estimate is pulled towards the middle of the observed effects
Removed the studies whose effects disagree with the others, so the remaining set is more internally consistent than before
options.misconception: invents an exclusion the model does not perform

options.text: Given each study the same weight, so no single large study dominates the pooled figure it has produced
options.misconception: describes equal weighting rather than variance-based weighting

options.text: Widened the search so that more studies were found, which is why the estimates differ between the two analyses
options.misconception: attributes a modelling difference to a different set of studies

questions.explanation: A random-effects model adds a between-study variance component to each study's sampling variance before computing the weights, and two things follow. The interval widens, because the pooled standard error now includes the spread of the studies around the average, and the weights shift away from the largest studies towards the smaller ones, so the pooled estimate moves towards the middle of the observed effects rather than towards the biggest one. Both changes are the point: the first says the evidence is less certain than a fixed model claims, and the second says the large studies have less influence on the average than the fixed model would give them. The pull towards 0.18 rather than 0.30 here is the shrinking towards the mean that a variance-based weighting produces, not an improvement in the evidence. Options B, C and D describe actions the model does not take.
questions.hint: Ask what was added to each study's variance before the weights were computed.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Measuring between-study heterogeneity
questions.learningObjective: state what a heterogeneity statistic measures
questions.stem: A review reports that the heterogeneity test gives a p-value of 0.11 across twelve studies. What is the correct reading of that number?

options.text: The observed spread is not clearly larger than chance would produce, which is weak evidence of consistency and not proof that the studies agree
The studies agree, because a p-value above the conventional threshold confirms the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity
options.misconception: treats failure to reject as confirmation

options.text: The review should pool only the largest studies, since small studies are what produce an insignificant heterogeneity test
options.misconception: invents a selection rule the statistic does not imply

options.text: Twelve studies are too few to assess heterogeneity, so the number should not have been reported at all
options.misconception: dismisses a reported statistic rather than reading what it says

questions.explanation: A heterogeneity test asks whether the spread between the study estimates is larger than their standard errors predict, and a p-value of 0.11 says this evidence is not strong enough to reject the null of no detectable heterogeneity, which is a statement about the strength of the evidence rather than about the state of the world. A small review genuinely lacks the power to detect moderate heterogeneity, so the same number would be far more informative in thirty studies than in twelve, and a report that pairs the test with a magnitude statistic such as the proportion of variance attributable to between-study differences lets a reader see the size rather than only the significance. That pairing is what stops the p-value being read as permission to pool. Option B is the error of treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence, options C and D each try to make the number mean something it does not.
questions.hint: Ask what the test failed to establish, not what it proved.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Reading an I-squared value
questions.learningObjective: interpret the proportion of variance that is between studies
questions.stem: A meta-analysis of ten studies reports an I-squared of 4 per cent, and a second analysis after removing three small studies reports 71 per cent. What does the second number indicate?

options.text: That the larger studies give estimates far more spread out than their own precision predicts, so a single pooled value now conceals a wide range of true effects
That removing the small studies introduced the heterogeneity, since those studies had been artificially suppressing the spread
options.misconception: locates the cause of heterogeneity in an action taken to inspect it

options.text: That the first analysis was invalid, because a heterogeneity level of 4 per cent cannot be produced by a real set of studies
options.misconception: treats a small heterogeneity value as evidence of a mistake

options.text: That the pooled estimate should be recalculated with equal weights, since weighting is what produced the spread between studies
options.misconception: attributes the spread to the weighting rather than to the studies

questions.explanation: An I-squared states the share of the total variance across the study estimates that cannot be explained by sampling error alone, so 71 per cent says that most of the variation between these studies is real variation between the effects they are estimating, and the single pooled figure is then a number that describes none of them in particular. The jump from 4 to 71 per cent is not a change in the studies, since the same studies remain, but a change in which studies carry the estimate: small studies with wide intervals contribute sampling variance that flatters the I-squared, and once they are gone the genuine disagreement between the larger studies becomes visible. The right response is to report the pooled estimate together with the range of effects and to look for a moderator that explains the spread, not to pick whichever version gives the tidier number. Options B, C and D each misattribute the cause of the statistic.
questions.hint: Ask what the percentage is a percentage of, and which studies were left in the room when it was computed.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Elements a forest plot must display
questions.learningObjective: specify the evidence a forest plot carries
questions.stem: A reviewer wants a forest plot that lets a reader check the pooled estimate rather than take it on trust. Which set of elements does that require?

options.text: Each study's estimate with its interval, the weight each study carried, the pooled estimate with its interval, and the axes and scale those numbers are drawn on
Each study's estimate and interval, the pooled estimate, and a caption naming the outcome, so the reader can see the direction of the finding
options.misconception: omits the weights and the scale, which are what make the layout checkable

options.text: A bar chart of the study estimates, the pooled estimate as a labelled line, and the number of studies, so the shape of the evidence is visible at a glance
options.misconception: substitutes a bar chart for the estimates and intervals a check requires

options.text: Only the pooled estimate with its interval and the study names, since the individual estimates are what produce a visual impression the reader should resist
options.misconception: removes the study-level evidence and leaves the reader nothing to check the pool against

questions.explanation: A forest plot is a display of an arithmetic argument, and each element carries a specific part of it: a study's point estimate and its interval show what that study's data support, the weight shows how much the study actually contributed to the pooled figure, the diamond carries the pooled estimate and its interval, and the scale fixes the reading so that equal horizontal distances mean equal changes in the effect measure, which is what allows a reader to see at a glance that a study contributing one per cent of the weight sits far from the pool. Missing the weights is the commonest defect, because a reader who cannot see that one study dominated the result is invited to read the plot as a consensus. Options B, C and D each remove one of the parts that let a reader check the calculation rather than admire it.
questions.hint: Ask which element tells the reader how much each study moved the pooled number.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A pooled estimate and its interval
questions.learningObjective: state what a pooled interval licenses a reviewer to claim
questions.stem: A meta-analysis reports a pooled odds ratio of 1.6 with a 95 per cent interval from 1.1 to 2.3. A writer concludes that the intervention roughly halves the risk of the outcome. Which conclusion is the interval able to support?

options.text: The interval excludes 1.0, so an effect in the reviewed population is supported, and the direction is that the intervention reduces risk, though the interval is wide enough to admit a much smaller benefit than 1.6
The interval excludes 1.0, so the effect is exactly 1.6 and the uncertainty is only a matter of rounding the reported figure
options.misconception: reads a central estimate as if the interval placed no constraint on it

options.text: The interval excludes 1.0, so the result holds in every population, because a pooled interval is not specific to the studies that produced it
options.misconception: extends a pooled estimate beyond the population the studies sampled

options.text: Nothing yet, because an interval that excludes 1.0 says only that the effect is not nil, and a reduction in risk is a different claim from a change in odds
options.misconception: dismisses a valid result for a distinction the measure itself cannot make

questions.explanation: On an odds ratio the null value is 1, so an interval of 1.1 to 2.3 excludes it and the data are not consistent with no effect, which is the minimum a pooled analysis can establish. A ratio above 1 on the odds of an unwanted outcome means the intervention lowers that outcome, so the direction of the finding is a reduction, and the width of the interval is the reason the headline cannot be a specific one: 1.1 and 2.3 are compatible with a benefit barely distinguishable from nothing and with one a long way from it, and a rounded claim of halving the risk imports a precision the data never supplied. Reporting the pooled figure with its interval, in the population the studies sampled, is the honest form. Options B, C and D each claim more than the interval carries.
questions.hint: Ask what value the null takes on this measure, and how much room the interval leaves.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A meta-regression and the moderator it tests
questions.learningObjective: identify what a meta-regression can and cannot establish
questions.stem: A meta-regression of eighteen studies finds that effect size falls as the length of the programme increases, with a slope whose interval excludes zero. What has been shown, and what has not?

options.text: The studies with longer programmes tend to report smaller effects, an association between study-level characteristics and estimates that is exploratory until it is tested outside the same set
Duration causes the effect to shrink, because a significant slope identifies a cause and only the direction of the argument is missing
options.misconception: turns an association between study characteristics into a causal claim

options.text: The pooled estimate should be recomputed separately for each duration band, because the slope proves the two bands are different populations
options.misconception: proposes a split that the exploratory slope has not licensed

options.text: The moderator is confirmed, because it was specified in advance, so the association no longer needs checking in new data
options.misconception: assumes pre-specification alone converts an association into a finding

questions.explanation: A meta-regression runs a regression across study-level estimates, and the coefficient says that studies with a longer programme reported smaller effects, which is an association among studies rather than a claim about what happens to a programme when it is lengthened, because the studies that ran longer may differ in every other respect that matters. Three specific cautions follow. The study is the unit, so with eighteen studies the analysis has little power and the interval around the slope is the honest measure of how little is known. A significant association found while examining many possible moderators is one of several tests run, so a pre-specified moderator deserves more weight than a discovered one. And any claim that the moderator explains the heterogeneity should be tested by seeing whether a stratified analysis reproduces the pattern, which is the only way to learn whether it holds outside the set that suggested it.
questions.hint: Ask what varied across the studies, and whether a shorter programme was ever randomly assigned.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Multiplicity in a subgroup analysis
questions.learningObjective: explain why many subgroup tests invite false findings
questions.stem: A review tests five pre-specified subgroups at the conventional five per cent level and reports that one is significant, and the report then treats that subgroup as the population the programme works for. What is the problem?

options.text: With five tests, a significant result is expected by chance about one time in four, so the lone significant subgroup is a candidate for replication rather than a conclusion about where the programme works
Nothing, because the subgroups were pre-specified, and a pre-specified test is protected against the multiplicity problem entirely
options.misconception: assumes pre-specification removes the chance of a chance finding

options.text: Nothing, because only one test was significant, and a single significant result among several is exactly what a significant result means
options.misconception: counts the significant tests as if significance were a proportion of them

options.text: The problem is the threshold, because a review should use a per-test level of one per cent whenever more than one subgroup is examined
options.misconception: prescribes a stricter threshold without addressing what the finding would then mean

questions.explanation: When a study looks in k places it will find something by chance with a probability of one minus 0.95 to the k, and for five places that is close to a quarter, so an isolated significant subgroup is the expected result of a family of tests about a quarter of the time. A pre-registration of the subgroups raises the value of the finding because it prevents the analyst from searching for the one that works, but it does not change the arithmetic of the search. What a review should do is report all the subgroups tested and their estimates with intervals, not only the significant one, and pre-specify any claim about effect modification for testing in a new data set, since a difference between subgroups is a claim about two estimates and not about the programme. Option B and option C both treat the counting as protective, and option D makes the threshold a formality.
questions.hint: Ask how often a family of tests of this size produces a significant result with no real difference behind it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Registering a report before the results are known
questions.learningObjective: state what a registered report commits an author to
questions.stem: A team submits a design, a full analysis plan and a claim about what they will conclude to a registry, and the registry accepts it before any data are collected. What does the commitment buy, and what does it leave open?

options.text: The design and the analysis are on the public record in advance, so a later departure is visible, while the conclusion itself remains conditional on what the data show
The conclusions are guaranteed, because a journal that accepts a registered report publishes the stated findings whatever they turn out to be
options.misconception: believes registration binds the result rather than the method

options.text: The peer review is complete, because a registry panel has already judged the design sound and the statistics adequate
options.misconception: confuses pre-registration with pre-review

options.text: The data become shareable, because registering the analysis commits the team to depositing everything the analysis used
options.misconception: assumes a methods commitment implies a data commitment

questions.explanation: A registered report separates the two things peer review normally mixes, the judgement about whether a question is worth asking and whether the design can answer it, which happens in the open before results exist, and the judgement about whether the result is interesting, which happens afterwards on a fixed analysis. Because the analysis plan is public in advance, a reader can see whether a reported analysis was the planned one, whether subgroups were added, whether an outcome was quietly replaced, and the disclosure of departures is a condition of publication rather than a matter of goodwill. The commitment is about method and not about result, so a null result from a registered analysis is publishable while a striking result from an unregistered one is not thereby made credible. Option B confuses registration with a promise of publication, option C with prior review, and option D with a data obligation.
questions.hint: Ask which half of the research process is fixed in advance, and which half is left to the data.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A proportion of variance that is between studies
questions.learningObjective: compute a heterogeneity proportion from study estimates
questions.stem: Three studies report effects of 0.10, 0.40 and 0.50, each with a standard error of 0.10. Compute the proportion of the variance across the estimates that is not sampling error, that is, one minus the degrees of freedom divided by the total sum of weighted squared deviations, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Each variance is 0.01, so each weight is 100, the mean of the three effects is 0.3333, and the weighted squared deviations sum to 100 times the sum of 0.0544, 0.0044 and 0.0278, which is 8.6667. There are two degrees of freedom for three studies, so the share not attributable to sampling error is 1 minus 2 divided by 8.6667, which is 0.7692 and rounds to 0.77. The reading is that about three quarters of the disagreement between these three estimates is real disagreement about the effect, which is why a single pooled number would misrepresent them, and it is worth noticing that three studies is a very thin basis for any proportion: the same data with slightly wider intervals would produce a much smaller figure without the underlying disagreement changing at all.
questions.hint: Weight the squared deviations from the mean, compare the total with the degrees of freedom, and take the remainder as a proportion of the total.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Converting a mean difference into a correlation
questions.learningObjective: convert an effect size between two metrics
questions.stem: A study reports a standardised mean difference of 0.80. Convert it to the point-biserial correlation with which a reader of the original scale would express the same finding. Give the value to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The conversion divides the difference by the root of its own square plus four, so 0.80 divided by the root of 4.64, which is 2.1541, gives 0.3714 and rounds to 0.37. The direction of the relationship is the same in both metrics and the ordering of studies is unchanged, but the sizes are not interchangeable, and a reader who reports 0.80 in a context that expects a correlation has overstated the association by more than a factor of two. The relationship between the two metrics also depends on the base rate of the outcome in the sample, which is the reason the conversion carries an assumption: the same 0.80 difference implies a different correlation where the outcome is common than where it is rare, and where a study reports a continuous outcome rather than a dichotomy the conversion is an approximation rather than an identity.
questions.hint: Divide the difference by the square root of its own square plus four.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Bias-correcting a standardised mean difference
questions.learningObjective: apply the small-sample correction to a standardised mean difference
questions.stem: A study with 20 participants per condition reports a standardised mean difference of 0.80. Apply the correction factor one minus three divided by four times the total sample size minus nine, and give the corrected value to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The total sample size is 40, so the correction factor is 1 minus 3 divided by 151, which is 1 minus 0.0199, and multiplying 0.80 by that factor gives 0.7841, which rounds to 0.78. The reason the correction exists is that a standardised difference computed from a small sample is upward biased, because the same sample that produces the estimate also inflates the pooled standard deviation denominator, and the bias is largest in exactly the studies with the fewest participants, which is why an unadjusted average of small studies overstates an effect. The adjustment is a one-line adjustment, but it does not repair what it corrects: a small study with a wide interval still contributes little to a pooled estimate, and the corrected figure should be reported with that interval rather than presented as a firmer number than the study earned.
questions.hint: Apply the factor to the reported difference; it is close to one but pulls the value down.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A pooled event rate across studies
questions.learningObjective: compute a pooled proportion from study counts
questions.stem: Four studies report 12 events in 200 participants, 25 in 300, 16 in 100 and 30 in 400. Give the pooled event rate as a proportion across all participants, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Adding the events gives 83 and adding the participants gives 1,000, so the pooled rate is 0.083, and the sum works because each study reports the same quantity in the same units. A simple average of the four study rates would be 0.095, and the gap between the two figures is the whole content of the item, since the average of rates gives the 100-participant study with the highest rate the same weight as the study with four times as many participants. The pooled figure is therefore not a neutral summary: it is an estimate for the combined population, and it is only the right summary when the studies are otherwise comparable, since a study of a higher-risk subgroup contributes its rate to a denominator that contains lower-risk participants too. Reading 0.095 as the answer is the natural error here, and it is an error about what an average is averaging.
questions.hint: Add the numerators and add the denominators, then divide once.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Share of identified records that reach inclusion
questions.learningObjective: compute the proportion of a flow that reaches inclusion
questions.stem: A review reports 1,200 records identified, 340 removed as duplicates, 860 screened, 705 excluded at screening, 155 assessed in full, 112 excluded in full, and 43 included. Give the number of identified records that reached inclusion as a proportion, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The numerator is the 43 included and the denominator is every record the search returned, which is 1,200, so the share is 43 divided by 1,200, or 0.0358, which rounds to 0.036. Using the 860 screened as the denominator instead would give 0.050, and that is the number to be careful about, because a search that returns a great many irrelevant records looks more thorough in that form while having been less precise, and the two quantities answer different questions about the search's behaviour. A flow of this kind is reported precisely so that both are visible: how much the search retrieved, how much survived the first filter, and how much survived all of them.
questions.hint: Take the studies included at the end and divide by every record the search returned at the start.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Records a Boolean combination can return
questions.learningObjective: count the combinations a search string can return
questions.stem: A search joins three bracketed groups with the keyword operator, and the groups contain 4, 3 and 2 search terms respectively, each term matched in a separate field. A record returns when it matches at least one term from every group. Give the number of distinct term combinations that can satisfy the string.
questions.explanation: Because the groups are joined by the keyword operator, a record qualifies by matching any term from each group, and the number of ways of choosing one term per group is the product of the group sizes, so 4 times 3 times 2 is 24. The product is the right construction precisely because of the disjunction inside each group and the conjunction between them, and it is the same arithmetic that makes the string's breadth grow multiplicatively: adding one synonym to the smallest group changes the number of combinations by a factor of three, which is why thesaurus work on a small group is more valuable than extra terms on a large one. It also explains why the count is a count of combinations rather than of records, since many records match several combinations and the database counts a record once.
questions.hint: Choose one term from each group; the choices are independent, so multiply the group sizes.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance of at least one significant result in a family of tests
questions.learningObjective: compute the false-positive chance across a family of tests
questions.stem: Four subgroup comparisons are each tested at the five per cent level, independently, and no real difference exists between the subgroups. Give the probability that at least one of the four is reported as significant, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Each test has a 0.95 chance of producing nothing significant when there is no difference, and independence makes the four such events multiply, so the chance that all four are unremarkable is 0.8145 and the chance that at least one is significant is 1 minus that, which is 0.1855 and rounds to 0.19. Nearly one study in five will report a significant subgroup from nothing but the search, which is why a review that quotes only the significant subgroup invites exactly the wrong conclusion. The remedies are to report every subgroup tested, to state in advance which comparisons are confirmatory, and to treat any claim about where an effect is larger as a claim to be tested in fresh data rather than a conclusion of the review.
questions.hint: Find the chance that all of them come back unremarkable, and subtract that from one.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Half-width of a pooled interval
questions.learningObjective: compute the precision of a fixed-effect pooled estimate
questions.stem: Four studies each report a standard error of 0.10, and a fixed-effect meta-analysis weights each by the inverse of its variance. Give half the width of the 95 per cent interval around the pooled estimate, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Each variance is 0.01 so each weight is 100, the weights sum to 400, and the standard error of the pooled estimate is the square root of the reciprocal of that sum, which is 0.05. Half the width of a 95 per cent interval is 1.96 times that standard error, so 1.96 times 0.05 is 0.098, and the full interval runs from the pooled estimate minus 0.098 to the pooled estimate plus 0.098. The instructive part is what the pooling has done to the precision: the individual intervals are 0.196 wide and the pooled one is also 0.196 wide, because four equally precise studies carry exactly the same information as one study of four times the size, so pooling four studies of a given precision buys no additional precision at all and its only benefit is a single combined estimate rather than four separate ones.
questions.hint: Add the inverse-variance weights, take the square root of the reciprocal for the standard error, then multiply by 1.96.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Choosing an outcome measure for a review
questions.learningObjective: evaluate whether an outcome measure supports the intended comparison
questions.stem: Studies in a review report the same programme's effect on three outcomes: waiting time, patient-reported satisfaction, and a laboratory measure of stress. Which consideration decides whether these can be pooled as one outcome?

options.text: Whether the three measure the same construct in the same direction and are recorded on a scale that can be put on a common footing, since a pooled figure is meaningless across different constructs
Whether all three were measured in every study, since a complete set of three is what the review set out to collect
options.misconception: confuses the review's data-collection plan with the identity of a construct

options.text: Whether the three were collected at the same moment in the programme, since timing is the only thing that makes outcomes comparable
options.misconception: reduces comparability to timing and ignores what each measure denotes

options.text: Whether the three have similar numbers, since outcomes on similar scales are the ones that can be combined
options.misconception: makes pooling a matter of the size of the numbers rather than their meaning

questions.explanation: Pooling is an arithmetic operation that assumes the quantities added are the same quantity, so the question that governs a meta-analysis of several outcomes is whether each instrument is measuring the same construct in the same direction, and if the instruments differ only in scale a conversion can sometimes be justified and should be shown, while if they differ in what they are sensitive to no conversion exists and the outcomes belong in separate analyses. Waiting time and patient satisfaction can even move in opposite directions under the same programme, so a naive pooling of them would produce a number with no referent at all. A review should therefore define one primary outcome in the protocol, treat the others as separate syntheses, and say in advance which will drive the conclusions.
questions.hint: Ask whether the three numbers denote the same thing, and whether they point the same way.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A sensitivity analysis that drops one study
questions.learningObjective: state what excluding a study in sensitivity analysis tests
questions.stem: A meta-analysis of 20 studies has a pooled estimate of 0.40. Removing the single largest study gives 0.12, and removing the smallest gives 0.39. What has the first result established?

options.text: That the pooled figure depends heavily on one study, so the summary should be reported with that dependence visible and the dominant study's influence examined rather than hidden
That the largest study was wrong, since a study whose removal changes the answer must have made an error
options.misconception: treats influence as evidence of error in the influential study

options.text: That the smaller studies are more trustworthy, since they agree more closely with the estimate that survives without the large one
options.misconception: prefers a subgroup because it leaves the estimate the reviewer prefers

options.text: That the pooled estimate should be reported as 0.12, since the analysis that excludes the largest study is the more robust of the two
options.misconception: selects the estimate that a robustness check was meant to interrogate

questions.explanation: A leave-one-out analysis asks a single question of every study in turn: does the summary survive without it, and a large movement on removal says that the summary is being carried by that study rather than supported by the body of evidence, which is a fact about the evidence that has to be reported. It does not follow that the large study is wrong, since a large, well-conducted, precise study deserves its weight and removing it is a hypothetical, but it does follow that the reader should be told the result without it, given its risk-of-bias rating and told what might explain the disagreement, and that the interpretation should be cautious rather than settled. Here the contrast is informative: dropping the smallest study barely moves the estimate while dropping the largest removes most of it, which locates the dependence precisely.
questions.hint: Ask what a study's removal does to the summary, and what that says about the summary rather than about the study.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The tension between open data and participant privacy
questions.learningObjective: state why open data is not simply a matter of releasing a file
questions.stem: A study's consent form says that individual responses will not be shared, and the funder requires that the data supporting the published claims be made available. What follows?

options.text: The commitment is about the material, so the data can be released only after removing or coarsening the information that identifies a participant, and the form's wording decides how far that can go
The funder's requirement overrides the consent, so identifying details can simply be removed and the remainder released without further thought
options.misconception: treats an external requirement as if it settled the participants' expectations

options.text: The two commitments are compatible already, because a dataset with no names attached cannot identify anybody
options.misconception: assumes a dataset free of names cannot identify anybody

options.text: Nothing can be shared, so the funder's requirement must be met with a description of the dataset rather than with the dataset
options.misconception: jumps to refusing release rather than to transforming the data

questions.explanation: Openness and confidentiality pull in opposite directions only when confidentiality is understood as a property of the data rather than of the promise, and the productive answer is to treat de-identification as a transformation with a cost: rows can be dropped, rare categories combined, ages banded, and free-text fields removed, and each of those steps reduces what a re-analysis can do, so the choice of which to accept is a scientific decision as well as an ethical one. What the consent form settles is the ceiling, because a participant who was told that individual responses would not be shared has been given a commitment, and releasing a file that makes them identifiable breaks it regardless of the funder's wishes. Rare categories and free text are where re-identification lives, which is why the standard practice is a documented transformation applied to a deposit that is then reviewed. Options B, C and D each skip the transformation or deny that it is needed.
questions.hint: Ask what the participants were promised, and what has to change about the file before that promise can be kept.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Exceptions claimed in a data-availability statement
questions.learningObjective: evaluate an exception claimed in a data-availability statement
questions.stem: A paper's data-availability statement says the data are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request, and names no repository. How should a reader treat that statement?

options.text: As the weakest available commitment, since the author's availability is not durable, the request may be refused, and a refusal leaves no trace that a reader could report
As an adequate commitment, because a named individual is a more reliable point of contact than an automated repository
options.misconception: prefers a personal channel to a durable one without a reason

options.text: As a commitment to unrestricted release, because a request-based channel is simply a slower route to the same file
options.misconception: reads a discretionary channel as though it granted access by right

options.text: As a technical impossibility, because the data contain participant information that cannot lawfully be transferred to anyone
options.misconception: converts an absent statement into an asserted legal bar

questions.explanation: A data-availability statement is a claim about what a reader will be able to do, and the strength of the claim is set by what it binds the author to rather than by how warmly it is worded. A named person with a discretionary channel satisfies none of the properties that make reuse possible: the person may have moved institutions, the request may be answered slowly or not at all, and nothing about the refusal is visible to anyone else, so a reader cannot distinguish a refusal from an attempt. A repository deposit with a persistent identifier, a licence and a stated access condition converts the claim into something a third party can check and something that survives the author, and where a deposit is genuinely impossible the statement should say so and say why. Options B, C and D each credit the statement with a commitment it does not make.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader can do if the named person leaves, declines, or is slow.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a licence permits on a shared dataset
questions.learningObjective: state what a licence does and does not settle about reuse
questions.stem: A dataset is deposited under a licence that permits anyone to copy, adapt and redistribute it provided the source is credited. What does that licence settle, and what does it leave to the user?

options.text: It settles the right to reuse and redistribute with attribution, and it leaves the user responsible for the ethics of the new use, including whether consent extends to it
It settles the right to reuse freely and removes any obligation the user has towards the participants the data describe
options.misconception: treats a permission from the depositor as a permission from the participants

options.text: It settles only the right to read the data, because any derivative work needs a further agreement with the depositor
options.misconception: narrows a reuse licence to read access

options.text: It settles the right to reuse and the obligation to cite, so a user who credits the source has discharged every requirement
options.misconception: confuses one condition with the whole of the ethical question

questions.explanation: A licence is a permission from the party that holds the rights, and it is silent about everyone else, so permitting reuse settles the copyright question and leaves the consent question exactly where it was. That is the distinction a user most often misses, since a dataset of identifiable or sensitive material can be lawfully reusable and ethically unusable in ways nobody authorised, and a derived dataset that republishes individual records in a new context is a new disclosure rather than a mechanical application of a permission. Reputable practice therefore treats the licence as the floor and the consent, the data-use agreement and the repository's access conditions as the remaining constraints, and a study that collected material under a specific and limited promise should not expect a broad licence to override it. questions.topic: The constraint a data-use agreement adds
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a licence from a data-use agreement
questions.stem: A repository hosts a dataset from a linked-data study. Reusers must sign an agreement naming their project, agree not to attempt re-identification, and accept that their outputs will be checked for compliance. How does that arrangement differ from a licence?

It is simply a licence with more pages, since both are permissions granted by the holder of the rights
options.misconception: collapses a conditional agreement into a general permission

options.text: It removes the ethical questions, because a signed agreement shows the depositor has considered how the data might be misused
options.misconception: assumes a signature settles the ethics of the use

options.text: It makes the data open, since anyone who completes the steps can obtain them and a process is not a restriction
options.misconception: confuses administrative steps with substantive constraints

questions.topic: A completeness claim the search log contradicts
questions.learningObjective: identify the contradiction between a claim and a recorded search

What is the fair reading?

The claim is supported, because a grey-literature repository also indexes non-English material and so the language coverage is secured

options.text: The claim is unsupported but harmless, because a review that declares its search is transparent even where the search fell short
options.misconception: defuses a false claim on the grounds that it was disclosed

options.text: The claim is true in substance, because searching two databases well is equivalent to searching many badly
options.misconception: equates depth of searching with breadth of sources

questions.topic: A pre-registration that omits an analysis
questions.learningObjective: explain what an unregistered analysis in a registered study means
questions.stem: A registered report states that the primary analysis is a comparison of two groups on a continuous outcome. The paper instead reports three groups with two pairwise comparisons and a subgroup split, and the largest effect appears between two of the subgroups. What has happened, and what should a reader do?

options.text: The primary analysis was replaced after the data were seen, so the largest effect is an exploratory result from a family of comparisons and is not the finding the registration licensed
The registration was extended, so the paper's analysis is a legitimate update of the plan and needs no comment
options.misconception: assumes a changed plan is automatically an approved amendment

options.text: The groups were combined for power, so reporting the finer comparison is a legitimate refinement of the planned analysis
options.misconception: invents a power motive that would in any case worsen the multiplicity problem

options.text: The registration covered outcomes rather than analyses, so the choice of comparison is outside what registration constrains
options.misconception: narrows a registration's scope to a single field it always includes

questions.explanation: A registration's value is that it fixes the analysis, so when the paper's analysis is not the one registered, the informative reading is that the choice was made with the data visible, and everything that follows from that choice carries the character of an exploration: a larger family of comparisons, no adjustment for the extra tests, and a headline effect drawn from whichever comparison came out largest. A reader should therefore treat that effect as a hypothesis, note the divergence from the registration as a finding about the study rather than as a detail, and look for whether the registered comparison is reported anywhere in the paper, because a study that keeps its registered analysis in the text has given the reader a real test and one that has quietly replaced it has not. Options B, C and D each excuse the substitution.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reported comparison is the one that was fixed before the data were seen.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A shareable data statement and what blocks it
questions.learningObjective: identify the practical obstacle behind a non-shareable claim
questions.stem: A team's data-availability statement says the data cannot be shared because the funder's award conditions prohibit it, and the raw data include free-text interview responses and precise locations. Which obstacle is actually operative?

options.text: Both, and a statement that names only the funder is incomplete, since the free text and the locations would remain a disclosure risk even if the award allowed release
Only the funder, because the risk in the file is a matter for the depositor's institution to resolve rather than for the data statement
options.misconception: clears the file of risk by assigning it elsewhere

options.text: Only the file, because a funder's restriction on release is a preference rather than a condition and can be declined
options.misconception: recharacterises a contractual condition as a preference

options.text: Neither, because free text and locations can be stripped out and the resulting file released under the funder's terms in a form the funder would accept
options.misconception: assumes the obstacles are simultaneously absent and resolvable without evidence

questions.explanation: A data-availability statement that lists one obstacle and stays silent about another is a partial disclosure that will be read as a complete account, and the obstacle it omits is the one that would survive a change of heart, since removing identifiers from a file that contains verbatim interview answers and precise locations does not remove what can be inferred about the people in them. Naming both is the accurate and more useful statement, because it tells a reader that a different funder's conditions would not by itself unblock the deposit, and it tells the authors what would actually have to change. Option B relocates a risk the statement is precisely about, option C understates the status of an award condition, and option D asserts a resolution that neither party has offered.
questions.hint: Ask what the statement would still say if the funder's restriction were lifted tomorrow.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A replication package that cannot be run
questions.learningObjective: specify what a replication package must contain
questions.stem: A replication package supplies the cleaned dataset, a document listing the variables, and a summary of the analyses reported in the paper, but not the code that produced them. What can a third party do with it?

options.text: They can read the data and re-derive the reported figures by hand, which is a partial check, but they cannot reproduce the pipeline, so every undocumented cleaning and model choice remains invisible
They can fully reproduce the analysis, because a data dictionary plus a list of the analyses specifies every step needed
options.misconception: mistakes a description of the analyses for a specification of their implementation

options.text: They can extend the study, because a cleaned dataset is the part of the work that matters most and the code is a convenience
options.misconception: inverts the value of the code relative to the data

options.text: They can verify the numbers, because any figure can be recomputed from the data by a competent analyst given the list of analyses
options.misconception: overstates what a verbal list of analyses supplies about the steps taken

questions.explanation: The part of a study that is lost when the code is not shared is the sequence of decisions, not the data, and those decisions are where a re-analysis diverges: which records were dropped, how missing values were filled, which model was fitted, which observations were excluded and when. A list of the analyses names the outputs and not the path to them, so a third party has to reconstruct a plausible path and cannot tell whether the path they reconstructed is the one the authors took. That is why the package for a computational result contains the data, the code that transforms and analyses it, the environment the code was run in, and a stated entry point, since the entry point is what makes the claim testable rather than aspirational. Options B, C and D each credit the package with a reproducibility it does not deliver.
questions.hint: Ask what a person who did the work would have to remember that the package does not record.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A pipeline that does not rerun
questions.learningObjective: distinguish computational from statistical reproducibility
questions.stem: A paper's code runs to completion on the deposited data, but a fitted model returns a coefficient of 0.31 where the paper reports 0.28. The paper's method section names the model family but not the link function or the solver settings. What does the rerun show?

options.text: That the code is executable but the specification is incomplete, so the discrepancy points at an undocumented modelling choice rather than at a broken pipeline or a wrong result
That the paper's figure is wrong, since a rerun that differs by three hundredths has identified an error in the published number
options.misconception: treats any discrepancy as a detected error

options.text: That the pipeline is not reproducible, because the only requirement for reproducibility is that the code runs without error
options.misconception: reduces reproducibility to successful execution

options.text: That the deposited data are not the data used, since matching figures are the only evidence that the right input was supplied
options.misconception: jumps to a data mismatch rather than to an unspecified step

questions.explanation: Computational reproducibility asks whether the deposited artefacts regenerate the reported result, and statistical reproducibility asks whether the reported result is determined by a fully stated method, and this rerun separates the two: the code executes, so the first holds, and the mismatch localises the failure to the second, because a coefficient that depends on a link function or a solver setting is not pinned down by naming a family. The remedy is specific and cheap, to record the link, the solver and its settings, the convergence criterion, the starting values where they matter and the software version, all of which are the kind of detail that is usually lost precisely because it was obvious to the author. A discrepancy of this size is a gift, since it shows a reader that the number was not determined by the method as written. Options B, C and D each collapse the diagnosis into a single verdict.
questions.hint: Ask whether the code ran, and separately whether the method fixes the number the code returns.

questions.topic: Who decides on access to a restricted repository
questions.learningObjective: identify where the decision on access is actually taken
questions.stem: A dataset is held in a repository whose access committee includes two researchers from the field, one statistician, one member of the original study's ethics committee, and no representative of the participants. An application that would link the data to a national administrative register is under consideration. Where does the substantive decision sit?

options.text: With the committee, whose composition means the linkage is judged on methodological and confidentiality grounds, and the absence of a participant representative is a gap in whose interests are represented
With the repository, since hosting the data makes it the natural owner of the decision about who may use them
options.misconception: assigns a hosting role to a policy decision

options.text: With the requesting team, since an application is a professional judgement and committees only rubber-stamp it
options.misconception: removes the review from a process that exists to check the judgement

options.text: With the funder, since the award conditions determine what the data may be used for and no other body can vary them
options.misconception: assumes the funder adjudicates individual applications

questions.explanation: Access decisions are substantive judgements about whether a proposed use stays inside the consent that was given, and the whole point of a committee is that the judgement is made by people who can weigh confidentiality against scientific value, which a repository cannot do on a requester's behalf and a funder is not set up to do case by case. The composition is therefore itself part of the answer, because an access process decides whose interests count when the use is a sensitive linkage, and a committee of researchers and methodologists is well placed to judge linkage validity while having no one speaking for the people whose records would be linked. That is a gap worth recording in the deposit's documentation rather than a reason to withhold the data. Options B, C and D each place the decision where no informed judgement sits.
questions.hint: Ask which body is set up to weigh a proposed use against the terms on which the data were collected.
